opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to understand it is that the foundation model and reinforcement learning play very different but complementary roles. The foundation model gives you the raw capability. Through pretraining on enormous amounts of internet data, the model already knows what a web page looks like, roughly how search works, how to read text, how to write a query, even how to reason a little. Without that base, there's no way RL alone could get you an agent that browses the web. The search space is just too large. If you start from a random policy and try to learn clicking and typing from scratch, you'll never get anywhere.

But having the capability in principle doesn't mean the model reliably uses it to accomplish a goal. A pretrained model, or even an instruction-tuned one, will often give up too early, trust the first result it sees, fail to cross-check, or lose track of what it was trying to do after many steps. That's where reinforcement learning comes in. RL is how you turn latent ability into goal-directed behavior. You give the model a task, let it actually interact with the environment over many steps, and reward it on whether it really got the answer right. Through that process it learns things that are very hard to teach through imitation: persistence, when to search again, how to verify, how to recover from a dead end.

So the analogy I like is that the foundation model decides the ceiling, and RL decides how close you get to that ceiling. A stronger base model means RL has much better behaviors to discover and reinforce. Strong RL on a weak model doesn't produce magic either. What we saw with these browsing and research agents is that once the base model got good enough, especially with reasoning abilities, end-to-end RL on real agentic tasks unlocked a big jump. Things like spending a long time searching, trying dozens of queries, and synthesizing information emerged because the training rewarded outcomes, not because someone hand-wrote those strategies.

There's also an engineering side people underestimate. For RL to work on web agents, you need good environments, tasks that are hard but verifiable, and infrastructure that supports long, multi-turn rollouts at scale. Much of the progress comes from getting that system right, not just the algorithm. But conceptually, pretraining gives you knowledge and priors, and RL teaches the model how to act on them.

r001.rationale: It says RL alone could not produce a web-browsing agent from scratch because the search space is too large; the foundation model supplies the needed base capability.

r002.rationale: It says having capability in principle does not mean the model can reliably accomplish a goal, and describes RL as turning that latent ability into goal-directed behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yi Wu: I think the way to look at it is that these are really two separate problems, and OpenAI solved them in a very particular order.

The first problem is: can the model even understand what a webpage is? Can it read a page, understand what the buttons mean, understand what "add to cart" implies, understand that this form is asking for a shipping address? That's a comprehension and world-knowledge problem, and that's almost entirely the foundation model's job. The pretraining on huge amounts of web data, plus the multimodal ability to look at screenshots, gives you a model that already "knows" what the internet looks like. If you don't have that, there's nothing to do reinforcement learning on. You'd be trying to teach an agent to navigate a world it can't perceive.

The second problem is: given that the model understands the page, can it actually take a sequence of actions over many steps and get to the goal? That's where reinforcement learning comes in. And I want to be careful here, because people sometimes think RL is doing the "intelligence" part. It isn't, really. The foundation model provides the prior, the common sense, the language ability. RL is doing something more like calibration and long-horizon credit assignment. It's teaching the model: when you clicked here, that eventually led to failure three steps later; when you scrolled down instead of guessing, that eventually led to success. A model trained purely on next-token prediction is very bad at that, because it was never optimized for consequences. It's optimized to say the plausible thing, not the thing that works.

So in practice, the base model gives you a policy that's maybe reasonable in a single step but drifts over long tasks. It gets stuck in loops, it hallucinates a button that isn't there, it declares success too early. RL on actual task outcomes, with real or simulated environments, fixes exactly those behaviors. You see the agent become much more patient, much more willing to verify, much more robust to pages that don't look like it expected.

There's also a feedback loop between the two that I think is underappreciated. The RL environments themselves generate data about which behaviors succeed, and that data goes back into shaping future models. So it's not foundation model first, RL second, done. It's iterative. The better the base model, the more sample-efficient the RL, because you're not wasting rollouts on basic mistakes. And the better the RL, the more useful trajectories you have to inform the next base model.

The hard part, honestly, is the environment and the reward. The web is open-ended, tasks are vague, and "did the agent succeed" is often a judgment call. A lot of the real engineering effort at OpenAI and elsewhere is not in the algorithm, it's in building environments that are realistic enough, and reward signals that are reliable enough, that RL doesn't just learn to exploit the grader. If you get that right, the combination of a strong prior plus outcome-based optimization is extremely powerful. If you get it wrong, you get an agent that looks great on the benchmark and falls apart on a real website.

r001.rationale: The response says the foundation model must understand and perceive webpages first, and that without this there is “nothing to do reinforcement learning on.”

r002.rationale: The response says a next-token-trained foundation model drifts on long tasks and is not optimized for consequences; it describes reinforcement learning as necessary to improve outcome-driven action sequences.

astra-6.text:
I think foundation models and reinforcement learning play complementary roles. The foundation model gives the agent a starting set of capabilities: understanding the user’s request, interpreting a webpage, and reasoning about what action might help. But being able to describe how to use a website is different from reliably completing a task on it.

That’s where reinforcement learning can help. The agent takes actions, observes what happens, and learns from whether it achieves the goal. For a web task, that might mean navigating several pages, filling out a form, noticing an error, and correcting it. The challenge is learning a sequence of decisions whose payoff may come much later.

So I’d think of the foundation model as providing the capabilities that make useful exploration possible, and reinforcement learning as shaping those capabilities into effective behavior through interaction. I wouldn’t claim to know OpenAI’s exact internal recipe, but that combination is how I’d understand the general approach.

r001.rationale: The response says the foundation model supplies the understanding and reasoning capabilities that make useful exploration possible, establishing its necessary role in web interaction.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes describing website use from reliably completing a task, then says reinforcement learning shapes the model’s capabilities into effective behavior through interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as complementary. The foundation model provides a starting point: it can understand instructions, interpret what’s on a web page, and draw on general knowledge to decide what actions might make sense. That gives you a broad set of capabilities, but it doesn’t automatically make a reliable agent.

Interacting with the web is a sequential decision problem. You take an action, the page changes, and you have to decide what to do next. Sometimes you make a mistake, sometimes the result is unexpected, and often you only know whether you succeeded at the end. Reinforcement learning can train the model on those interactions, so it learns to choose actions that lead to successful task completion, recover from errors, and check whether it has actually achieved the user’s goal.

So the foundation model gives you the initial capability, and reinforcement learning helps turn that capability into effective behavior over many steps. I’m describing the general relationship here; I wouldn’t claim to know the specific details of OpenAI’s training setup.

r001.rationale: The response says the foundation model provides the initial capability and reinforcement learning turns that capability into effective behavior, communicating that RL depends on a capable foundation model.

r002.rationale: The response says foundation-model capabilities do not automatically make a reliable agent and that reinforcement learning helps make them effective over multiple steps.
